pg008_n0005: This textbook, Book-keeping for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg008_n0006: The book is prepared in accordance with the 2023 Book-keeping Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MoEST).
pg008_n0007: It is a revised edition of Book-keeping for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form One that was published in 2022.
pg008_n0009: The book consists of seven (7) chapters, namely Introduction to Book-keeping, Basic principles of Book-keeping, Application of the double entry system, Recording of business transactions, Ledgers, Trial balance, and Basic financial statements.
pg008_n0010: In addition to the contents, each chapter contains activities, illustrations, exercises, and revision exercises.
pg008_n0011: You are encouraged to do all activities and exercises as well as other assignment provided by your teacher.
pg008_n0012: You are also required to prepare a portfolio for keeping record of activities perfomed in different lessons.
pg008_n0013: Doing so will enable you to develop the intended competencies.

pg009_n0007: Book-keeping equips students with essential skills and knowledge vital for their future careers.
pg009_n0008: When students master Book-keeping principles and concepts, they will gain a solid foundation for understanding financial transactions and record them accurately.
pg009_n0009: A strong understanding of Book-keeping knowledge and skills empowers students to contribute effectively to both financial success in business arena and in managing personal financial matters.
pg009_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn concept of Book-keeping by focusing on the origin, meaning, scope, purpose, types of Book-keeping methods or systems, relationship with other disciplines and basic terms used in Book-keeping.
pg009_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to appreciate the importance of keeping business financial transactions and have ability to negotiate and reason effectively during business deals.

pg009_n0019: One of the common occupations that form an important part of day-to-day income generation in any country is business.
pg009_n0020: Although, many businesses are also conducted by large companies both locally and internationally, a significant number of people in business are involved in small businesses.
pg009_n0021: We interact with small businesses every day in the process of buying our daily needs.
pg009_n0022: Typical small businesses include hawkers, vegetable vendors, street retail shops, shoe shining, newspaper vending, salon businesses (hair dressers), artisans and many others.
pg009_n0023: All these businesses make different financial transactions, involving buying inputs or materials, doing some processing, and selling their goods or delivering services.
pg009_n0025: Book-keeping is a necessary process for any business enterprise.
pg009_n0026: Business operators or owners without the proper knowledge of Book-keeping will somehow unknowingly apply Book-keeping principles in order to achieve various objectives of their
pg010_n0004: Take an example of Mrs Chaza who starts a food vending business by the name of Swahili-bites.
pg010_n0005: This business operates near Jenga-afya Secondary School in Maruku.
pg010_n0006: The business will need equipment like cookers, pans and serving utensils.
pg010_n0007: It will also need some furniture like benches, tables and cupboards.
pg010_n0008: It will buy raw food and cook it for sale.
pg010_n0009: To ensure that the food business runs successfully, Mrs Chaza might be required to do the following:
pg010_n0012: (i) Hire some cooks and service attendants,
pg010_n0018: (iv) Receive cash from sales made, and
pg010_n0020: (v) Record credit sales (in case some food is sold on credit).
pg010_n0022: All these activities will involve movement of money.
pg010_n0023: Eventually, Mrs Chaza would need to evaluate whether the business is achieving its objectives.
pg010_n0024: One of the likely objectives is to make a profit from such operations.
pg010_n0025: This means that Mrs Chaza will need to calculate whether her business has generated a profit or not.
pg010_n0026: To be able to determine the profit or a loss, some calculations will have to be done by comparing the sales (revenue) made from selling food against the costs of materials and services used.
pg010_n0027: To do this, there would be a need to keep records of money paid on each material and services, as well as money received from selling food to customers.
pg010_n0028: Simply put, the process of keeping records of money spent on each material and service as well as money received from selling goods to customers is what is known as “Book-keeping”.
pg010_n0032: The origin of Book-keeping can be traced back to the ancient civilisations like Sumeria and Egypt.
pg010_n0033: These societies developed systems to record and track transactions and goods exchanged.
pg010_n0034: Overtime, Book-keeping principles advanced to various techniques through contributions from Greeks and Romans entrepreneurs.
pg010_n0035: In the medieval period, Luca Pacioli in 1494 played a significant role in promoting double entry Book-keeping system.
pg010_n0036: This introduction was a significant development that revolutionised the field of Book-keeping.
pg010_n0037: Since then, Book-keeping has continued to evolve, adapting to changing economic systems and technological advancements.
pg010_n0038: As we speak, Book-keeping remains a vital part of accounting and financial management, ensuring maintenance of records, facilitating financial reporting, analysis, and maintaining transparency and accountability in financial affairs.
pg010_n0042: Book-keeping is an important part of the accounting process.
pg010_n0043: It plays an important role in the early stages in the accounting process.
pg010_n0044: As explained earlier, Book-keeping can be defined as the art of recording business financial transactions in the books of accounts in an orderly manner.
pg010_n0045: In principle, every transaction has to be recorded in a systematic
pg011_n0004: Such recording includes proper classification according to the nature of the transaction.
pg011_n0005: The end result of Book-keeping is to have net figures or balances in the ledger accounts.
pg011_n0006: This will help to determine a profit or a loss and the financial position of the business.
pg011_n0007: Book-keeping also helps in the management of credit dealings, proper control of the business and appropriate computation of taxes.
pg011_n0008: Hence, Book-keeping is the systematic recording, organising and tracking of financial transactions and activities within a business.

pg011_n0018: The process of Book-keeping covers the recording, classification, organisation and maintenance of records of financial transactions.
pg011_n0019: It plays central role in providing accurate financial information for decision making, legal and regulatory compliance and financial analysis within a business.
pg011_n0023: The purpose of Book-keeping is to enable business to record and track the financial transactions of an enterprise or business activities.
pg011_n0024: Book-keeping provides clear and organised records of business financial transactions, including sales, purchases, consumption, payments and receipts.
pg011_n0025: The specific purposes of Book-keeping include:
pg011_n0029: Financial records: Book-keeping ensures all financial records are properly documented and easily accessible when needed.
pg011_n0030: It provides a comprehensive record of financial transactions, which helps in maintaining a clear and accurate account of the enterprise’s financial activities.
pg011_n0033: Compliance and legal requirements: Book-keeping plays a crucial role in fulfilling legal and regulatory obligations.
pg011_n0034: Organised and appropriate financial records are necessary for preparing tax returns and, meeting financial reporting requirements.
pg011_n0037: Financial management: Book-keeping provides information for effective financial management.
pg011_n0038: It enables businesses to track expenses, monitor cash flow, and evaluate financial resources.
pg011_n0039: By having up-to-date financial records, an enterprise can make informed decisions regarding investment, budgeting and resource allocation.
pg011_n0042: Facilitating business decision making: Book-keeping provides insights into revenue generation, cost management, and profitability.
pg011_n0043: The information helps in making sound business decisions.
pg012_n0005: Management with accurate financial data can analyse different aspects of the business, identify areas for improvement, and make strategic decisions to drive business growth.
pg012_n0009: Book-keeping is important to business owners and other parties outside the enterprise in the following ways:
pg012_n0013: Book-keeping helps a business to determine whether it is making a profit or a loss.
pg012_n0014: This is possible because Book-keeping helps the enterprise to keep complete, accurate and up-to-date financial records that are used in preparing financial statements.
pg012_n0015: Take an example of Mrs Chaza on page 2 Book-keeping assists the business to calculate profits or losses made for any period from the food vending business.
pg012_n0019: Many businesses are conducted on both cash and credit basis.
pg012_n0020: For example, Mrs Chaza, would sell most of its food for cash, but she would occasionally sell to some customers on credit.
pg012_n0021: Similarly, it is possible that Mrs Chaza buys some of its raw foods on credit from the market.
pg012_n0022: In practice, many businesses have a significant volume of transactions conducted on credit.
pg012_n0023: Book-keeping helps the enterprises to maintain appropriate records of their credit transactions and know the amount due from each of its debtors and the amount owing to each of its creditors.
pg012_n0024: Such records can systematically be kept following Book-keeping principles.
pg012_n0027: Debtor: This is a customer who has bought goods on credit from business and promises to pay at a later date.
pg012_n0029: Creditor: This is a supplier who sold goods or provided service on credit to the business for payment to be made at a later date.
pg012_n0033: To have an effective control of a business, the owner of the business needs to keep proper records of his or her financial matters.
pg012_n0034: These records, in the long run, help the owner to decide on matters such as expansion or reduction of the business.
pg012_n0035: If Mrs Chaza sells breakfast, lunch and dinner; appropriate record keeping may assist in deciding on the extent of efforts to dedicate to each of the menus.
pg012_n0036: Additionally, in case the food is sold from more than one location or centre; Book-keeping may suggest whether the volume in one or another centre may need to be expanded or reduced according to the sales records.
pg012_n0037: Book-keeping can also help the proprietor to see whether there are possible incidences where money, foodstuff or materials have been stolen or misused.
pg012_n0038: This can be useful in making a decision on the corrective measures to be taken where necessary.
pg013_n0005: Book-keeping helps the owner to determine the financial position of his or her enterprise.
pg013_n0006: It enables him or her to understand the value of assets, liabilities, and the amount of capital contributed by the owner.
pg013_n0007: This can be useful in establishing whether the business has grown or not.
pg013_n0008: Knowing the financial position of a business can also assist in applying for a loan or other form of credit for expanding its operations.
pg013_n0012: Tax authorities such as the Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA) and Zanzibar Revenue Authority (ZRA) need to receive and examine the books of accounts of every enterprise operating in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg013_n0013: This is important in calculating the amount of tax that should be paid by the enterprises.
pg013_n0014: Tax laws in Tanzania use self-assessment system, where for some taxes the taxpayer is required to make own calculation of tax payable.
pg013_n0015: Thus, proper keeping of financial records helps both the owner and tax authorities to assess the amount of tax payable.
pg013_n0016: Tax laws in Tanzania also penalise businesses that do not maintain financial documents and records properly.
pg013_n0017: Book-keeping therefore, may help the business save money that would otherwise be paid as penalties for not maintaining financial records.

pg013_n0027: The determination of a profit or a loss, together with other objectives, is done through the preparation of financial statements.
pg013_n0028: The entire process that businesses undertake to prepare financial statements from accounting records is known as the accounting cycle.
pg013_n0029: The accounting cycle involves eight stages, and Book-keeping plays an active role in the first seven.
pg013_n0030: The stages in the accounting cycle are summarised as follows:
pg013_n0034: Identifying transactions using the source documents,
pg014_n0004: (ii) Recording the transactions in the books of prime entry,
pg014_n0006: (iii) Posting transactions to the ledger accounts,
pg014_n0010: (v) Making adjusting entries and correction of errors,
pg014_n0016: (viii) Analysing and interpreting the financial statements.
pg014_n0018: Identifying transactions and recording in source documents
pg014_n0020: This is the first stage in the accounting process where financial transactions are identified and evidenced through source documents such as receipts, payment vouchers, invoices, cheques, debit note and credit note.
pg014_n0021: For a transaction to be identified and evidenced, it must be of a financial value and it must affect at least two items of the accounting equation.
pg014_n0023: Recording the transactions in the books of prime entry
pg014_n0025: The second stage is to record such transactions in the books of prime entry, which are also known as books of original entry.
pg014_n0026: The transaction is initially recorded in these books before it is recorded or posted anywhere else.
pg014_n0027: This book will focus on six types of books of prime entry, namely a sales journal, a purchases journal, a sales returns journal, a purchase returns journal, a general journal, and a cash book.
pg014_n0029: Posting transactions to the ledger accounts
pg014_n0031: The third stage in the accounting cycle is posting transactions to the ledger accounts.
pg014_n0032: This process involves the posting of entries that were initially recorded in the books of prime entry to the ledger accounts.
pg014_n0033: The posting of entries to the respective ledger accounts is done by following the double entry system of Book-keeping.
pg014_n0037: The fourth stage in the accounting cycle is the extraction of the trial balance.
pg014_n0038: The trial balance is a list prepared at a specific date showing net figures or balances of all general ledger accounts.
pg014_n0039: The account balances extracted from the general ledger are listed in the debit and credit columns of the trial balance.
pg014_n0040: The debit and credit columns must balance.
pg014_n0041: The trial balance is usually prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of double entries made to the ledger accounts, and it acts as a compiled list of balances for use in the preparation of financial statements.
pg014_n0045: This is a summarised record of business transactions.
pg014_n0046: It can be presented on a page of a ledger book.
pg014_n0049: These are two terms which are used in describing the two sides of an account, that is, the left-hand side (Debit) and the right-hand side (Credit).
pg015_n0003: Double entry: This is the system or principle of Book-keeping whereby each business transaction is recorded in the book of accounts.
pg015_n0005: Making adjusting entries and correction of errors
pg015_n0007: A trial balance is expected to reveal some errors made when transactions are first entered in the books of prime entry or when double entry is done in the ledger.
pg015_n0008: These errors need to be corrected.
pg015_n0009: This is a process that goes together with making any necessary adjustments of the balances before the preparation of financial statements.
pg015_n0013: After correcting the errors and making adjusting entries, the adjusted trial balance will need to be prepared.
pg015_n0014: This is the one that has balances that are used in the preparation of financial statements.
pg015_n0018: Financial statements are prepared using figures extracted from the adjusted trial balance.
pg015_n0019: The aim of preparing the financial statements is to know the performance, financial position and cash flows of the enterprise.
pg015_n0020: This includes determining whether the enterprise is making profits or losses (usually done through preparing an income statement) and to show the financial wealth of the enterprise.
pg015_n0021: This is done through the statement of financial position.
pg015_n0023: Analysing and interpreting the financial statements
pg015_n0025: The financial statements need to be analysed and interpreted to assess the performance of the enterprise.
pg015_n0026: This is done in comparison with other enterprises, as well as the progress made from one period to another.
pg015_n0027: One of the tools used for analysing financial statements is ratio analysis.
pg015_n0028: Analysed financial information is useful to several users such as owners, lenders and creditors in making informed decision.
pg015_n0032: Modern Book-keeping uses double entry system.
pg015_n0033: However, some businesses still find it adequate to use a single entry system.
pg015_n0034: The following are the two systems of Book-keeping:
pg015_n0038: Double-entry Book-keeping is a more comprehensive and widely used method that provides a more accurate and detailed representation of business's financial transactions.
pg015_n0039: It follows the principle that every transaction has equal and opposite effects on at least two accounts.
pg015_n0040: Each transaction is recorded with a debit entry in one account and an equal credit entry in another.
pg015_n0041: This method maintains a system of accounts, including assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses.
pg015_n0042: Double-entry book-keeping ensures that the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) remains balanced and allows for the preparation of accurate financial statements such as statement of financial position and income statements.
pg016_n0003: (ii) Single-entry Book-keeping: Single-entry book-keeping is a simple and straightforward method primarily used by small businesses or individuals with relatively few repetitive and uncomplicated financial transactions.
pg016_n0004: In this method, only a single entry is made for each transaction, typically in a revenue or expense journal or a cash book.
pg016_n0005: It records income and expenses, but it does not track individual accounts for assets and liabilities.
pg016_n0006: Single-entry book-keeping is used for basic record-keeping purposes such as tracking cash receipts and payments.
pg016_n0007: These two types of Book-keeping methods differ in complexity and the level of financial details they provide.
pg016_n0008: While single-entry Book-keeping is suitable for small businesses with straightforward transactions, double-entry Book-keeping is the standard method used by most businesses due to its accuracy, reliability, and ability to provide a comprehensive financial overview.

pg019_n0012: Relationship between Book-keeping and other disciplines
pg019_n0014: Book-keeping supports operationalisation of other disciplines.
pg019_n0015: The knowledge and skills acquired in Book-keeping are also applicable in different subject areas covered in the Ordinary Secondary Education Curriculum and beyond.
pg019_n0016: The relationship that exists between Book-keeping and some other disciplines is explained as follows:
pg019_n0020: Book-keeping lays down the foundation of the Accountancy subject.
pg019_n0021: It deals with recording and posting entries to various ledgers that are used by accountants to analyse, interpret and make informed
pg019_n0022: Accountants produce reports popularly known as financial statements.
pg019_n0023: These financial statements are prepared using balances that are generated from the ledgers, which are prepared by book keepers.
pg019_n0024: Financial information is important for business management, investments, tax assessment, and government regulations activities.
pg019_n0025: Therefore, without the knowledge of Book-keeping, it would be difficult, for accountants to prepare and analyse financial statements.
pg019_n0029: Book-keeping provides skills for preparing manufacturing accounts and how to accumulate various costs which are related to commercial activities.
pg019_n0030: The relationship between Business Studies and Book-keeping lies in their business activities which result in financial generation.

pg019_n0036: Also, Book-keeping develop skills for maintaining economics records, calculating national income, performing cost analysis and production costs.
pg019_n0037: Both disciplines contribute to the effective financial management and informed economic decision-making.

pg020_n0006: It helps individuals and families to effectively manage their resources, making informed financial choices and achieve their financial goals.

pg020_n0012: Computer scientists contribute by creating accounting software, ensuring data integrity, implementing security measures, utilising artificial intelligence to prepare financial statements and reports.

pg020_n0036: Book-keeping is a fundamental concept in financial management, involving the systematic recording, organising, and summarising of information about financial transactions.
pg020_n0037: Its origins can be traced back to ancient civilisations where basic record-keeping practices were employed.
pg020_n0038: Today, Book-keeping has evolved into a structured discipline with defined principles and techniques.
pg020_n0040: The purpose of Book-keeping is to provide a basis for a clear and accurate representation of business's financial activities.
pg020_n0041: It encompasses tasks such as recording transactions, classifying them into appropriate accounts, and generating financial statements.
pg020_n0042: Book-keeping plays a vital role in supporting decision-making by providing insights into cashflows, assets, liabilities, revenue, and expenses.
pg020_n0043: It also ensures compliance with legal and
pg021_n0003: regulatory requirements, facilitates financial analysis, and enhances transparency and accountability.
pg021_n0005: Within the realm of Book-keeping, various terms are commonly used in describing key concepts.
pg021_n0006: These include assets (the resources owned by a business), liabilities (the debts or obligations), revenue (the income generated), expenses (the costs incurred), accounts receivable (amounts owed to the business by its customers), accounts payable (amounts owed by the business to its suppliers), cashflows (the movement of cash), journals (chronological records of transactions), ledgers (individual account records), and financial statements (such as statement of financial position and income statements).
pg021_n0007: Familiarity with these terms is crucial for accurate record-keeping and effective financial management.

pg023_n0006: The monetary measurement principle states that only transactions or events that can be expressed in monetary terms should be included in the accounting records.
pg023_n0007: This principle implies that only measurable and quantifiable economic events should be recognised and reported in the financial statements.
pg023_n0008: Items that can not be quantified in monetary terms are not recorded in financial statements.

pg023_n0016: The going concern principle, also known as the continuity assumption, assumes that a business will continue its operations beyond a reasonable length of time it will not be forced to liquidate or cease operations in the foreseeable future.
pg023_n0017: This principle underlies the preparation of financial statements and the basis for valuing assets and liabilities.

pg023_n0021: The going concern principle is significant in assessing the financial health and viability of a business.
pg023_n0022: Financial statements prepared using this principle provide information to users about the enterprise’s ability to meet its financial obligations, continue operations, and generate profits in the long term.
pg023_n0023: However, if circumstances arise that raise doubts about the business’s ability to continue as a going concern, such as significant financial difficulties or legal issues, the going concern principle may be questioned.
pg023_n0024: In such cases, additional disclosures or adjustments may be required to reflect the potential impact on the financial statements.
pg023_n0026: The going concern principle ensures that financial statements reflect the assumption of business continuity.
pg023_n0027: It also allows stakeholders to make informed decisions based on the assumption that the enterprise will continue its operations in the foreseeable future.
pg023_n0031: The time period principle, also known as the periodicity concept, suggests that the
pg024_n0003: financial activities of a business should be divided into specific and meaningful time periods for reporting purposes.
pg024_n0004: This principle allows for the systematic and regular preparation of financial statements, providing timely and relevant information to users.
pg024_n0006: Under this principle, the financial year is divided into shorter periods, such as months, quarters or years, depending on the reporting requirements and industry practices.
pg024_n0007: Financial transactions and events are recorded and summarised within these designated time periods, enabling the preparation of interim and annual financial statements.
pg024_n0008: The time period principle helps to facilitate the analysis and comparison of financial information over different periods.
pg024_n0009: By breaking down the financial activities into uniform time intervals, it allows stakeholders to assess the business’s performance, identify trends, and make informed decisions based on up-to-date information.
pg024_n0013: This is a fundamental accounting principle that guides the recognition of expenses in financial statements.
pg024_n0014: It states that expenses should be recognised and recorded in the same accounting period in which they are incurred to generate revenue.
pg024_n0015: The principle aims to achieve a proper matching of expenses with the revenues earned during a specific period.
pg024_n0016: This provides a more accurate representation of the business’s financial performance.
pg024_n0021: Expenses should be recognised when the related revenue is recognised:
pg024_n0022: When a business earns revenue from the sale of goods or the provision of services, it should also recognize the expenses directly associated with generation of that revenue in the same period.
pg024_n0023: This ensures that the costs incurred to generate revenue are properly matched with the revenue in the financial statements.
pg024_n0026: Expenses should be recognised in a systematic and rational manner.
pg024_n0027: The matching principle requires expenses to be recognised in a logical and consistent manner over the accounting periods.
pg024_n0028: It discourages the recognition of expenses only when payment is made or received.
pg024_n0030: By following the matching principle, businesses can provide more accurate meaningful measure of performance.
pg024_n0031: It allows users of financial statements to assess the profitability and financial performance of a business by matching the expenses directly to the revenues they helped to generate.

pg025_n0008: This is a fundamental accounting principle that determines when and how revenue should be recognised or recorded in the financial statements.
pg025_n0009: It provides guidance on when to recognize revenue and how to measure it.
pg025_n0010: It also ensures that revenue is reported accurately and in the appropriate period.
pg025_n0011: According to the revenue recognition principle, revenue should be recognised when it is both realised or realisable and earned.
pg025_n0012: This occurs when the following criteria are met:
pg025_n0016: Identification of the contract: There should be a legally enforceable agreement between the seller and the buyer, outlining the rights and obligations of both parties.
pg025_n0019: Delivery of goods or services: The seller has transferred control of the goods or services to the buyer.
pg025_n0022: Determination of the transaction price: The transaction price is determined and can be reasonably estimated.
pg025_n0023: It includes consideration received or expected to be received from the buyer in exchange for the goods or services.
pg025_n0026: Collectability probability: It is probable that the seller will collect the amount he or she is entitled to receive from the buyer.
pg025_n0028: Once these criteria are met, revenue should be recognised in the accounting records.
pg025_n0029: The amount recognised is typically the fair value of the consideration received or receivable in exchange for the goods or services provided.
pg025_n0030: The revenue can be recognised at a point in time (for example, when the goods are delivered) or over time (for example, as services are performed).
pg025_n0031: It is important to note that specific industries or transactions may have additional guidance or standards for revenue recognition, such as long-term construction contracts or software sales.
pg025_n0032: These industry-specific rules may provide further criteria or guidelines to determine when revenue should be recognised.
pg025_n0034: In summary, the revenue recognition principle insists on recognising revenue in the books when activities involving sale of goods or service have reasonably been performed, amount is known and has been collected or is reasonably expected to be collected.

pg026_n0023: The materiality principle states that financial information should be reported and disclosed if it has the potential to influence the decision-making of users of the financial statements.
pg026_n0024: Materiality is determined by the nature and amount of an item or event.
pg026_n0025: If an item or event is significant to impact the assessment or evaluation of a business’s financial position, performance, or cash flows, it should be disclosed in the financial statements.
pg026_n0026: The materiality principle recognises that not all financial information is of equal importance.
pg026_n0027: It allows accountants to focus on reporting information that is relevant and significant, while avoiding excessive detail that may not affect the decision-making process.
pg026_n0028: Allowing excessive details may crowd the important information that would be the focus of the users of accounting information.
pg026_n0029: This principle encourages someone to exercise professional judgment in determining material information that requires clear and transparent disclosure in the financial statements.
pg026_n0030: Information is therefore material if its inclusion or omission in the financial statements can affect the decision of the users of financial statements.
pg026_n0032: The materiality principle acknowledges that financial statements should present a true and fair view of a business’s financial position and performance.
pg026_n0033: It enables users to make informed decisions based on the significant factors affecting the business’s financial outcomes.
pg026_n0034: Applying the materiality principle requires someone to exercise professional judgment, considering both quantitative and qualitative factors.
pg026_n0035: Accountants must consider the impact of an item or event on
pg027_n0003: the financial statements and the potential influence it may have on the decisions of users.
pg027_n0005: By considering materiality principle, financial statements can provide a balance between the need for comprehensive and accurate reporting and the practicality of focusing on information that is most relevant and significant to the users of the financial statements.
pg027_n0009: Historical cost accounting is an accounting principle that states that, assets should be recorded and reported at their original cost when acquired by an enterprise.
pg027_n0010: According to this principle, the initial cost of an asset represents its value, regardless of any changes in market value over time.
pg027_n0011: In this principle, when an enterprise acquires an asset, it is recorded on the financial position statement (balance sheet) at the price paid to acquire or produce the asset.
pg027_n0012: This cost includes the purchase price and any additional costs incurred to bring the asset to its present condition and location, such as transportation costs and installation fees.
pg027_n0014: The rationale behind the historical cost principle is to provide a reliable and objective basis for financial reporting.
pg027_n0015: By using the original cost of an asset, financial statements reflect the actual resources expended by the enterprise at the time of acquisition.
pg027_n0016: This principle promotes consistency and comparability in financial statements.
pg027_n0017: It avoids general estimates of an asset’s value and prevents manipulation of reported figures based on market fluctuations.
pg027_n0019: However, critics argue that the historical cost principle may not provide a relevant and accurate representation of an asset’s true value, particularly for long-lived assets like property, plant, and equipment.
pg027_n0020: Over time, the market value of assets may change due to factors such as inflation, technological advancements, or changes in market conditions.
pg027_n0021: Some alternative valuation methods, such as fair value accounting, attempt to address these limitations by valuing assets at their current market value.
pg027_n0022: Despite its limitations, the historical cost principle remains widely used in financial reporting, especially for assets that do not have determined market values.
pg027_n0023: It provides a conservative approach to valuing assets and is considered a fundamental principle in traditional accounting practices.
pg027_n0024: Historical cost principle is in line with the going concern principle.
pg027_n0028: This principle states that once an accounting method or principle has been chosen and applied, it should be consistently used for similar transactions and events in subsequent periods.
pg027_n0029: In other words, an entity should not change its accounting methods or principles arbitrarily from one period to another, as it can create confusion and make it difficult to compare financial information across different periods.
pg028_n0003: Consistency in accounting allows for better comparability of financial statements, enabling users to make meaningful comparisons and assessments of an entity’s financial performance and position over time.
pg028_n0004: If a change in accounting methods or principles is deemed necessary, it should be accompanied by proper disclosure and justification, typically in the notes to the financial statements.
pg028_n0005: It is important to note that the consistency principle does not mean that accounting methods cannot be changed or updated.
pg028_n0006: Changes in accounting standards, regulations, or circumstances may require adjustments to accounting methods.
pg028_n0007: However, any changes should be made with careful consideration and with the aim of improving the relevance and reliability of financial information.
pg028_n0011: Prudence, also known as the conservatism principle, is an important concept in Book-keeping and accounting.
pg028_n0012: It suggests that when faced with uncertainty or doubt, accountants should exercise caution and choose the option that is more conservative or prudent.
pg028_n0013: In other words, it is better to make mistakes on the side of understating assets and revenues or overstating liabilities and expenses rather than overstating assets and revenues or understating liabilities and expenses.
pg028_n0019: It is important to note that the prudence principle should be applied judiciously and should not be used as a justification for intentionally understating assets or income or overstating liabilities or expenses.
pg028_n0020: The principle aims to strike a balance between caution and providing a true and fair view of an entity’s financial position and performance.
pg028_n0022: Dual aspect or the duality principle
pg028_n0024: In Book-keeping, the dual aspect or duality principle is a fundamental concept in accounting that forms the basis for the double-entry Book-keeping system.
pg028_n0025: According to the duality principle, every financial transaction has two offsetting effects.
pg028_n0026: Each transaction affects at least two accounts, with equal effects that cancel each other.
pg028_n0027: This principle recognises that every transaction involves a give-and-take relationship.
pg028_n0028: This is the foundation of the double entry principle that has become
pg029_n0003: a strong principle applied in the field of accounting.
pg029_n0007: This is an accounting system whose application promotes accuracy and reliability in recording financial transactions.
pg029_n0008: It is used in maintaining systematic and balanced records of an enterprise’s financial transactions.
pg029_n0009: Double entry system follows the fundamental principle that every financial transaction has dual effects on enterprise's accounts.
pg029_n0010: This means that for every debit entry recorded, there must be an equal and corresponding credit entry.
pg029_n0011: Double-entry system provides a more comprehensive view of an enterprise's financial position.
pg029_n0012: It also allows for better analysis and facilitates the preparation of more detailed financial statements.
pg029_n0016: Single entry system is sometimes called single entry Book-keeping.
pg029_n0017: It is a simplified Book-keeping method used by small businesses or individuals to track their financial transactions, primarily cash transactions.
pg029_n0018: This is different from double entry system which follows the principle of recording every transaction with at least two entries.
pg029_n0019: Single entry system makes a single entry for each transaction.
pg029_n0020: Single-entry Book-keeping may be simpler and more accessible for small businesses with straightforward financial transactions; the system lacks capacity to deal with records of large entities with varieties of transactions and high volume of trade.
pg029_n0022: As businesses grow or become more complex, they often change from single-entry system to double-entry system to ensure better financial control and reporting.

pg030_n0024: Relevance of accounting concepts and principles in Book-keeping
pg030_n0026: The relevance of accounting concepts and principles in Book-keeping is to improve the communication of financial information in language that is acceptable and understandable among enterprises.
pg030_n0027: The principles promote uniformity in the preparation of financial statements, making it possible for persons to compare the financial performance and position of different enterprises.

pg030_n0036: Going concern principle and the historical cost concept
pg030_n0038: The assumption of a going concern has an effect on the values of assets and liabilities that are reported in the financial statements.
pg030_n0039: When thinking about the figure to be reported for different assets in the financial statements, a business has to avoid looking at the value such that each asset can be sold in the market at present time.
pg031_n0003: This is because doing so will reflect an assumption that the assets are held for the purpose of being sold rather than for the purpose of being used in a business.
pg031_n0004: Reporting assets at market value would be appropriate when the business is expected to be closed in the near future (That is, within the next 12 months) or the business is no longer a going concern.
pg031_n0005: The historical cost concept makes this possible by prescribing that assets should be reported at their historical cost unless there are reasons to conclude that the business is no longer a going concern.
pg031_n0007: Going concern concept and the accounting period concept
pg031_n0009: The going concern principle literally assumes no end in the lifespan of a business.
pg031_n0010: It means that one would have to wait up to the end of the business to determine a profit or a loss.
pg031_n0011: Because of the need to know the performance of the business, the life of the business is divided into uniform accounting periods at the end of which financial statements are prepared and presented.
pg031_n0012: In this way, the going concern principle is observed, but without affecting the ability of the business to measure its performance.
pg031_n0014: Accounting period concept and the matching principle
pg031_n0016: As already defined, the accounting period is reflected in the act of dividing the life of a business into a uniform length of accounting periods.
pg031_n0017: It is known that at the end of each period, the performance of the entity is measured by matching revenue and expenses.
pg031_n0018: If there was no uniformity in the period covered by expenses and the one covered by revenue, then there would not be any meaningful profit or loss reported.

pg042_n0082: The accounting equation is the foundation of the concept of double entry.
pg042_n0083: Double entry deals with the recording and posting of business transactions in the books of accounts.
pg042_n0084: Business transactions are posted to ledger accounts following principle of double entry.
pg042_n0085: This section will explain the meaning of double entry and the principle of double entry.
pg042_n0086: Lastly, it will explain the importance of double entry.
pg042_n0090: Double entry system of Book-keeping records each transaction by making two corresponding entries in the books of accounts.
pg042_n0091: The reason for making two corresponding entries in the books is to simultaneously take into account the two effects of each transaction on the accounting equation.
pg042_n0092: The entries are therefore made so that they cancel each other to reflect the two effects on the accounting equation.
pg042_n0093: By doing this, the accounting equation would balance at any point in time.
pg042_n0094: Entries are made into two sides of the respective accounts representing a specific asset, liability, revenue, expense or capital to record increases and decreases following rules of debit and credit.
pg042_n0096: An increase in an asset is recorded by a debit entry in the specific asset account, whereas a decrease in an asset is recorded by an entry in the credit side of the asset’s account.
pg043_n0004: This rule is applied in recording increases and decreases in assets as a starting point.
pg043_n0005: It also find out the debit and credit rules for the rest of the elements in the accounting equation.
pg043_n0006: For example, liabilities are on the opposite side of assets in the accounting equation; therefore, increase in a liability will be recorded on the credit side of the specific liability account, while a decrease in a liability is recorded by a debit entry in its account.
pg043_n0008: The same reasoning will be used for the rest of the items or elements in the accounting equation.

pg047_n0085: The use of the double entry system is important in accounting process due to the following reasons:
pg047_n0087: Makes it easier to show the two effects of each transaction
pg047_n0089: The double entry system of Book-keeping requires every transaction to be recorded twice.
pg047_n0090: That is, every debit entry should have its corresponding credit entry.
pg047_n0091: For this reason, the double entry system of Book-keeping makes it easier for anyone analysing the business transaction to understand which of the two items or accounts have been affected by the transaction.
pg048_n0003: Assures arithmetic accuracy in the accounts thus minimising the possibility of errors
pg048_n0005: Since the double entry system of Book-keeping requires every debit to have a corresponding credit entry, the arithmetic accuracy of the books of accounts is assured.
pg048_n0006: The arithmetic accuracy in the accounts is further assured by the preparation of the trial balance periodically or at the end of the accounting period.
pg048_n0008: The basis of the balances used in preparing the financial statements
pg048_n0010: Balances used in preparing the trial balance and eventually in the financial statements are extracted from ledger accounts.
pg048_n0011: It should be noted that the posting of entries in the ledger accounts follows the double entry system of Book-keeping.
pg048_n0012: In this regard, double entry system ensures the preparation of the trial balance and financial statements.
pg048_n0014: Ensures that financial records are kept properly
pg048_n0016: Double entry ensures that financial records are kept permanently and properly in the books of accounts.
pg048_n0017: This is because entries in the ledger accounts are posted using the double entry system of Book-keeping.

pg048_n0032: The principle of double entry is a fundamental concept in accounting and book-keeping.
pg048_n0033: It ensures that every financial transaction has an equal and opposite effect on at least two accounts.
pg048_n0034: This system is widely used in maintaining accurate and balanced financial records.
pg048_n0035: By following the double entry system, businesses can achieve logically organised records that can be used in preparing financial statements.
pg048_n0036: This, in turn, enables them to analyse their financial performance, financial position and cashflow make informed decisions, and meet reporting requirements.
pg048_n0037: The application of the principle of double entry provides a strong and consistent framework for recording financial transactions, helping businesses to maintain a clear and accurate representation of their financial activities and facilitating effective financial management.

pg052_n0010: Recording of transactions in the books of accounts is the initial and very critical stage in accounting.
pg052_n0011: Correctness of the first record (prime or original) in the books of accounts for a transaction is the basis for having appropriate accounting records.
pg052_n0012: In this chapter, you will learn books of prime entry and preparation of such books.
pg052_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to prepare books of prime entry according to the required principles.
pg052_im001: Thinking face icon for a reflection activity
pg052_n0018: Operating a business without recording its financial transactions.
pg052_n0022: Books of prime entry, also known as books of original entry or daybooks, form an essential part of the double-entry accounting system used by businesses to record their financial transactions.
pg052_n0023: These books serve as the first point of entry for all the business transactions before they are posted into the ledger or processed further towards
pg052_n0028: Meaning of books of prime entry
pg052_n0030: Books of prime entry (journals) are the books of accounts that are used to record
pg053_n0003: any transaction for the first time.
pg053_n0004: In the books of prime entry, each transaction is recorded with as much detail as possible, in order to provide information concerning the transaction.
pg053_n0005: The name journal is adopted from a French word for diary.
pg053_n0006: It is therefore, a good practice to record transactions in the books of prime entry in a chronological order.
pg053_n0007: Transactions are also recorded as soon as possible from the time they occur to avoid situations where they may be forgotten or have their source documents misplaced.
pg053_n0008: For example, suppose Eliza sold three office chairs to Abraham for TZS 100,000 per office chair on credit.
pg053_n0009: In this case, Eliza is expected to record that she sold three office chairs for TZS 100,000 each to Abraham on credit.
pg053_n0010: Eliza is also expected to record the address and contact information of Abraham and the date of the transaction.
pg053_n0011: She would also record the details of the invoice issued to Abraham.
pg053_n0013: Types of books of prime entry
pg053_n0015: Books of prime entry are also known as journals or day books, except for a cash book.
pg053_n0016: These books are commonly termed as special journals or daybooks because they are used to record transactions of specific type on the daily basis.
pg053_n0017: There are six types of books of prime entry as presented below:
pg053_n0038: Use of books of prime entry
pg053_n0040: As already explained, there are six types of books of prime entry.
pg053_n0041: As their names suggest, each book serves its own purpose.
pg053_n0042: The following are brief descriptions and purpose of each of the book of prime entry:
pg053_n0046: The purchases daybook is used to record transactions related to credit purchases of goods.
pg053_n0047: In other words, this journal is used to record details of goods bought by the business with the promise that payment will be made in the future.
pg053_n0048: Cash purchases of goods are not recorded in this book.
pg053_n0052: The sales daybook is used to record transactions related to credit sales of goods.
pg053_n0053: This journal is used to record details of goods sold on credit with the promise that payment will be received in the future.
pg053_n0054: Cash sales of goods are not recorded in this book.
pg053_n0058: This daybook is used to record details of transactions related to sales returns, or returns of goods from customers to whom goods were sold on credit (debtors).
pg053_n0059: Each entry made include details of the goods and the credit note, the name of customer (debtor) and the amounts involved.
pg054_n0005: The purchase returns daybook is used to record transactions related to purchase returns, or return of goods to suppliers who supplied goods on credit (creditors).
pg054_n0006: Each entry made include details of the goods and the credit note, the name of supplier (creditor) and the amount involved as well as the reason of returning the goods.
pg054_n0010: The cash book is used to record transactions related to receipt and payment of cash as well as money placed into the bank (bank deposits) and those taken from the bank (bank withdrawals).
pg054_n0012: A cash book is a book of prime entry used to record transactions that involve movement of cash, that is receiving or paying cash by the business.
pg054_n0013: Since cash is an asset for the business, receipts of cash are recorded by a debit entry in the cash book (increase in assets), and payment of cash is recorded by a credit entry in the cash book (decrease in asset).
pg054_n0014: The cash book has a unique characteristic because, apart from being classified as a book of prime entry, it also forms part of a general ledger.
pg054_n0015: This is because some small businesses that operate strictly on cash basis find it easy to skip journals and instead, enter all transactions (receipts and payments) in the cash book.
pg054_n0016: For such businesses, when completing the corresponding entries to the other ledger accounts; they refer to that as posting.
pg054_n0018: A cash book is a financial record used to track cash and bank transactions in a business or enterprise.
pg054_n0019: It serves as a primary accounting register for cash receipts and cash payments.
pg054_n0020: The cash book records all inflows and outflows of cash, providing a complete and up-to-date record of the enterprise's cash position.
pg054_n0021: The cash book can be maintained in both manual and electronic formats.
pg054_n0022: In manual systems, it is often a physical book where transactions are recorded by hand, whereas in electronic systems, it is a digital record within a specific accounting software or any electronic spreadsheet.
pg054_n0023: A cash book can take different forms ranging from single column cash book, two column cash book, three column cash book and petty cash book.
pg054_n0024: For the purpose of this book, the focus will be on single column cash book.
pg054_n0028: This cash book has a single column used to record all cash or bank transactions.
pg054_n0029: Cash receipts, such as sales or loans received, are recorded on the debit side (left hand side) of the book.
pg054_n0030: While cash payments, such as expenses or loan repayments, are recorded on the credit side (right hand side) of the book.
pg054_n0034: This book of prime entry is used to record transactions related to other items, which according to their nature are not recorded in any of the books of prime entry.
pg054_n0035: It is important to note that businesses that do not have credit sales and purchases, or do not allow returns of goods may have all transactions recorded in the general
pg055_n0004: In any case, a business may record all transaction on the general journal, as long as it has in place a memorandum records to track specific details such as creditors and debtors details.
pg055_n0008: The information recorded in the books of original entry is taken straight from the documents that may either have been issued by the business or by its suppliers.
pg055_n0009: These documents are called source documents, because they are the source of information for recording transactions in the books.

pg055_n0015: Money could be received from customer for cash sale of goods or services.

pg055_n0017: Usually, the cash receipt contains information regarding the date of receipt, name or details of the customer, description of the item sold, quantities and the price of the product.
pg055_n0018: It also bears signature or stamp of the receiver of the money, and the amount received.
pg055_n0019: If the money received is for settlement of an account receivable, the receipt may also include the invoice number that identifies the sales invoice of the transaction.

pg062_n0010: As per the accounting cycle or process introduced in chapter one; once transactions are identified, they are entered in the books of prime entry, followed by posting the entries to relevant ledger accounts.

pg062_n0017: When goods are purchased on credit, the seller will prepare and send an invoice to the buyer.
pg062_n0018: The buyer will record this transaction in the purchases daybook because the transaction involves a credit purchases, meaning that the buyer did not pay for the goods at the time of purchase.
pg062_n0019: Therefore, the purchases daybook is used to record transactions relating to credit purchases of goods.
pg062_n0020: Practically, entries made in the purchases journal are summed up periodically (For example monthly).
pg062_n0024: The purchases daybook has six columns which are:
pg062_n0028: This column is used to write the date, the month, and the year of the transaction.

pg062_n0032: This column gives a short description of the entry for the transaction recorded.
pg062_n0033: It records the name of the supplier and the details of the items purchased.
pg062_n0036: This column records pages of reference in books of accounts.
pg062_n0037: It indicates in what ledger and on what page the transaction has been posted.
pg062_n0040: This column records the details of the invoice number which identify the invoice received when a particular transaction was made.
pg062_n0041: This is helpful for verifying or investigating errors in the records.
pg062_n0042: It makes it possible to retrieve the invoices (which are normally filed in a systematic manner) and match with the figures recorded in the books.
pg062_n0045: This column records the details of the invoice involved in the transaction, and it is especially useful where an invoice includes more than one type of goods.

pg067_n0028: Sales returns daybook or sales returns journal
pg067_n0030: There is time when goods sold to the customer are returned to the seller.
pg067_n0031: Goods might be returned by the customer due to several reasons including late delivery, low quality goods, different types or specifications (colour or size), damaged goods, expired goods or excessive quantity (oversupplied).
pg067_n0033: When a customer returns goods to a supplier, the supplier prepares and issues a credit note as an acknowledgement for the receipt of goods returned.
pg067_n0034: The purpose of the credit note is to inform the customer that his or her account has been credited to reduce the amount that was debited to the customer’s account at the time of sale.
pg067_n0035: In this case, a credit note serves as a source document, and it is used in the preparation of the sales returns daybook.
pg067_n0036: The sales return journal has the following columns:
pg068_n0005: This column is used to write the date, month, and year of the transaction.

pg068_n0010: This column indicates a short description of the entry for the transaction recorded.
pg068_n0011: It records the name of the customer, item and reason for returning the goods.
pg068_n0015: This column records pages of reference in books of accounts.
pg068_n0016: It indicates in what ledger and on what page the transaction has been recorded.
pg068_n0020: This column records the details of the credit note number which identifies the credit note issued when the return took place.
pg068_n0021: This is helpful for verifying or investigating errors in the records, because it makes it possible to retrieve the credit notes (which are normally filed) and match with the figures recorded in the books.
pg068_n0025: This column records the details of the credit note involved in the return and is useful where a credit note includes more than one type of goods returned.
pg068_n0029: This column records the amount of money being transacted, that is, the price of the goods returned.

pg073_n0020: The general journal is a book of prime entry used to record business transactions that are not recorded in special journals.
pg073_n0021: The other name of the general journal is the journal proper, and these names can be used interchangeably.
pg073_n0022: Examples of entries recorded in the general journal are entries for:
pg073_n0025: (a) Purchases or disposal of business assets not meant for sale.
pg073_n0029: (c) Adjustments of balances prior to the preparation of financial statements,
pg073_n0033: (e) Opening entries used in determining capital of an ongoing business that did not use double entry before.
pg073_n0035: The focus will be on the examples of the purchase of assets and opening entries.
pg073_n0036: The remaining items will be covered later in higher forms.
pg073_n0037: The general journal specifies the double entries (debit and credit entries) required to be made in respect of different transactions following the rules of debit and credit.
pg073_n0038: As noted earlier, it is possible for the general journal to be used to record all kinds of transactions conducted by the business.
pg073_n0039: This is because it gives direct guidance of the accounts and sides to which entries could be posted.
pg073_n0041: However, in case a business owner decides to use only a general journal, and happens to have some dealings on credit (sales, purchases, and returns), he or she will need to have some memorandum records (schedules) of the details of such dealings.
pg074_n0003: reason, entries in the general journal should be focused towards a general ledger.
pg074_n0004: In other words, it is not common to find the general journal entry made in relation to an individual account of a debtor or a creditor.
pg074_n0008: A general journal has the following functions:
pg074_n0012: It acts as a diary where business transactions are recorded as soon as they occur.
pg074_n0015: It gives the directions on which accounts should be debited and credited in respect of each transaction, following the rules of double entry.
pg074_n0018: It provides brief narrations of each transaction recorded.
pg074_n0019: This is very important because as opposed to the special journals, this journal records different types of transactions.
pg074_n0022: Since the transactions are recorded chronologically and include brief narrations, it is easy for a person to review and identify any possible errors that may have been made when recording.

pg077_n0095: Records of business transactions encompass the systematic documentation of all financial activities and events undertaken by an enterprise.
pg077_n0096: These records are vital for maintaining accurate and comprehensive accounting information, which serves as the foundation for financial management, analysis, and decision-making.
pg077_n0097: Each transaction is recorded in chronological order, supported by source documents such as invoices, receipts, and bank statements, providing evidence and ensuring transparency in the financial process.
pg077_n0098: By adhering to the principle of double entry, businesses ensure that their financial records are balanced and reliable.
pg077_n0099: These records facilitate the preparation of financial statements including components such as the statement of financial position, income statement, and cash flow statement.
pg077_n0100: They are also useful in audits, tax reporting, and compliance with regulatory requirements.
pg078_n0003: Maintaining accurate records of business transactions is crucial for business owners and managers to gain insights into the enterprise’s financial performance.
pg078_n0004: These records enable businesses to monitor cash flow, track revenue and expenses, and identify trends and potential areas for improvement.
pg078_n0005: Additionally, detailed records of transactions support strategic decision-making by providing real-time financial data and performance metrics, helping businesses identify opportunities and mitigate risks effectively.
pg078_n0006: By utilising modern accounting software and automation tools, businesses can streamline the record-keeping process by reducing manual errors.
pg078_n0007: They can also increase efficiency, and ensure that critical financial information is securely stored and easily accessible for informed business planning and growth.

pg083_n0008: Ledgers plays a crucial role in accounting and financial management for enterprises.
pg083_n0009: They serves as a key component of the accounting process, because the balances from ledgers form contents of financial statements.
pg083_n0010: Posting of entries to the ledger involves posting the entries to both subsidiary and general ledgers.
pg083_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn concept of a ledger and the posting of entries to the ledgers.
pg083_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to post entries from various books of prime entries to respective ledger accounts and balance the ledger accounts.

pg083_n0023: Concept of a ledger is fundamental to accounting.
pg083_n0024: A ledger is a principal book or digital record where business transactions are systematically and chronologically recorded.
pg083_n0025: It serves as a permanent and comprehensive repository of all transactions.
pg083_n0026: It provides a clear and organised picture of the enterprise's balances that will be used in determining financial performance and position.
pg083_n0027: This section presents the meaning of a ledger, types of ledgers, the importance of ledgers, the classification of accounts and the posting of entries to the ledger.
pg083_n0029: Meaning and format of a ledger
pg083_n0033: Ledger is a book used to record transactions.
pg083_n0034: It is used for keeping track of expenses, revenue, receipts, payments, and other financial matters.
pg083_n0035: It is, therefore, a record in which accounts are kept.
pg083_n0036: The ledger is often referred to as the main book of accounts.
pg083_n0037: This is because balances that are used for the preparation of financial
pg084_n0004: Entries of different transactions are posted to the ledgers from the books of prime entries.
pg084_n0005: The posting is done to specific accounts in the ledgers.
pg084_n0009: A ledger contains specific records called accounts.
pg084_n0010: An account is a record which shows increases and decreases of a specific asset, liability, revenue, expense or capital item in the ledger.
pg084_n0011: The ledger account has two sides.
pg084_n0012: These are the left-hand side, which is called the debit side (abbreviated as Dr.) and the right-hand side which is called the credit side (abbreviated as Cr.).
pg084_n0013: For the purpose of recording important details, each ledger account must has a name or title.
pg084_n0014: Additionally, each side of the ledger account has the following columns:
pg084_n0020: This column is used to write the date, month, and year of the transaction.
pg084_n0025: This column indicates the short description of the entry for the transaction recorded.
pg084_n0026: In the ledger account, this column indicates the name of the account to which the corresponding entry has been made for the transaction (remember the principle of double entry).
pg084_n0031: This column records pages of reference in books of accounts.
pg084_n0036: This column records the amount of money being transacted.
pg084_n0038: The format of the ledger account is presented as follows:
pg084_n0076: There are two main types of ledgers which are subsidiary ledger and the general ledger:
pg084_n0080: A subsidiary ledger is a ledger that contains accounts of individuals for the purpose of recording transactions between the entity and each individual.
pg084_n0081: The most common subsidiary ledgers are sales ledger and purchases ledger.
pg084_n0082: However, different enterprises may have some other subsidiary ledgers depending on the volume of transactions and
pg085_n0003: the need for details on different classes of transactions.
pg085_n0004: The sales and purchases ledgers are explained as follows:
pg085_n0008: A sales ledger is a subsidiary ledger used to record transactions, regarding credit customers, also known as debtors.
pg085_n0009: Therefore, the sales ledger comprises individual accounts of debtors.
pg085_n0010: The other names for debtors’ accounts are accounts receivable or trade receivables.
pg085_n0011: The sales ledger can also be referred to as the accounts receivable ledger, debtors’ ledger or trade receivables ledger.
pg085_n0015: A purchases ledger is a subsidiary ledger used to record transactions with creditors or suppliers of goods or services on credit.
pg085_n0016: A purchases ledger comprises individual accounts of creditors.
pg085_n0017: The other name for creditors’ accounts is accounts payable or trade payables.
pg085_n0018: The purchases ledger can also be referred to as the accounts payable ledger, creditors’ ledger or trade payables ledger.
pg085_n0022: The general ledger contains different accounts that do not record transactions relating to individuals.
pg085_n0023: Instead, it deals with total amounts from day books or special journals, or postings from the general journal to accounts that represent each class of transactions, namely revenue, expenses, assets, liabilities and owners’ equity (capital).
pg085_n0024: Posting of entries to the general ledger follows the double entry principle and form the basis of balances used in preparing financial statements.
pg085_n0025: A general ledger includes the cash book, which in some cases is also regarded as a book of prime entry.
pg085_n0026: A general ledger may also include other ledgers such as the private ledger.
pg085_n0030: There are ledgers that directors would not want their staff to see due to confidentiality.
pg085_n0031: These types of ledgers are called private ledgers.
pg085_n0032: A private ledger is a ledger used to keep confidential information of the business owner.
pg085_n0033: In this regard, the owner restricts access to the ledger to selected individuals.
pg085_n0034: Examples of private ledgers are capital ledger, and drawings ledger.
pg085_n0038: Every enterprise needs to post financial transactions in ledgers as they play important roles as follows:
pg085_n0040: They enable double entry to be completed
pg085_n0042: The double entry principle requires every transaction to be recorded twice.
pg085_n0043: That is, every debit entry must have its corresponding credit entry.
pg085_n0044: The posting of entries in ledger accounts follows the principle of double entry.
pg085_n0045: Posting entries to the ledger facilitates completion of double entry because a ledger account has a debit and a credit side, to which debit and credit entries are posted respectively.
pg085_n0047: They are used in the classification of accounts
pg085_n0049: Usually, accounts are classified into two categories.
pg086_n0004: The preparation of ledgers enables the book-keeper to classify accounts easily according to their nature.
pg086_n0006: Information extracted from a balanced ledger can be used for statistical purposes
pg086_n0008: Balances extracted from ledger accounts can be used as inputs for further analysis and projections concerning the firm.
pg086_n0009: These balances can also be used for statistical purposes as inputs by researchers who are researching on business enterprises or the industry where the enterprise is operating.
pg086_n0011: They are used to keep financial records permanently
pg086_n0013: Financial transactions posted on ledger accounts are permanent and cannot be altered.
pg086_n0014: This enables the owner and any others who may have access to the ledgers such as auditors and government authorities to make a reference of any transaction recorded in the ledger accounts.
pg086_n0015: Government authorities, for example, may need to review the financial records of the enterprise when investigating a particular transaction relating to illegal business.
pg086_n0017: They are used in the preparation of a trial balance
pg086_n0019: A ledger balance forms the basis for the preparation of a trial balance.
pg086_n0020: In simple terms, there is no trial balance if there are no general ledger accounts.
pg086_n0022: They provide information that is used as inputs when preparing the financial statements
pg086_n0024: Financial information that is used as inputs in the preparation of financial statements originate from ledgers.
pg086_n0025: Therefore, balances extracted from the ledgers make the preparation of financial statements possible.
pg086_n0029: This is the process of grouping accounts with similar nature and characteristics.
pg086_n0030: The posting of entries from both general and special journals involves opening different ledger accounts.
pg086_n0031: Different types of ledger accounts influence the way such accounts affect the financial statements.
pg086_n0032: It is, therefore, important at this stage to discuss the types of accounts.
pg086_n0033: There are two main types of accounts, namely personal accounts and impersonal accounts.
pg086_n0038: These types of accounts record transactions relating to persons.
pg086_n0039: There are two types of persons; a natural person and an artificial person.
pg086_n0040: A natural person is a person who was born biologically.
pg086_n0041: Examples of natural persons are Juma, Asha, and Anna.
pg086_n0042: On the other hand, an artificial person is the one formed under the law and empowered to perform activities (including business) in their own name, within the powers given to them by the law.
pg086_n0043: Examples of artificial persons are: Tanzania Institute of Education and Kijiko Sports Club.
pg086_n0044: The law treats an artificial person in the same manner as a natural person.
pg086_n0045: Therefore, such entries are recorded under the category of accounts known as personal accounts.
pg087_n0005: These are types of accounts that record all other transactions except those recorded in personal accounts.
pg087_n0006: They do not record transactions relating to persons or firms.
pg087_n0007: Impersonal accounts are further classified into real accounts and nominal accounts as follows:
pg087_n0011: These accounts record transactions relating to assets and liabilities in the general ledger.
pg087_n0012: These accounts are real because they are not closed at the end of the accounting period, their balances are carried forward to the next period.
pg087_n0013: Examples of real accounts include accounts for assets such as land and buildings, machinery, furniture and fittings, Motor vehicles, accounts receivable, cash at the bank and cash in hand.
pg087_n0014: Others include, liabilities such as accounts payable, bank overdrafts and bank loans.
pg087_n0018: Nominal accounts record transactions relating to expenses and revenues.
pg087_n0019: Expenses are costs incurred for running a business.
pg087_n0020: Examples of such expenses are rent, salaries, purchases, carriage, advertising, discounts allowed and bad debts.
pg087_n0021: Moreover, revenues are earnings of a business.
pg087_n0022: Examples of revenues are sales, creditors’ discount, interest income, and commission income.
pg087_n0023: Accounts falling under this category are closed at the end of the accounting period with their figures transferred to the income (profit or loss) statement.

pg088_n0070: Posting of entries to a ledger follows the double entry principle of Book-keeping.
pg088_n0071: For the case of a general journal, the journal entry would have already specified the name of the accounts and amounts to be debited and credited for each transaction.
pg088_n0072: In case of day books or special journals, the journal entries do not give direct guidance on accounts to be debited and credited.
pg088_n0073: This means that for day books or special journals, one will have to determine the nature of transactions recorded in the journal and use that to apply double entry rules as to debiting or crediting the relevant ledger account.
pg088_n0075: The nature of transaction will be dictated by the nature of the journal and the name used in the journal.
pg088_n0076: This will in turn dictate the ledger accounts to which the journal entries will be posted.
pg088_n0077: When posting, a consideration will be made on the nature of the account and the effect of the transaction as follows:
pg088_n0081: The posting will be made depending on what element of the accounting equation is affected by the transaction.
pg088_n0082: It is therefore important to identify whether the account to be posted is for assets, liabilities, revenue, expenses or owner’s equity (capital).
pg088_n0086: Once it is known which element is affected by the transaction, it is important to establish whether the transaction involves an increase or a decrease in that element.
pg088_n0087: This will help to decide whether the account identified in (a) above will be debited or credited.
pg089_n0004: An important feature of posting from special journals is that the entries are posted in two stages, namely posting to subsidiary ledger and posting to the general ledger.
pg089_n0005: These are illustrated by the subsequent explanation on posting from each special journal that immediately follows.
pg089_n0008: The sales journal records credit sales of goods to customers.
pg089_n0009: These transactions lead to the increase in revenue (sales) and increase in assets (trade receivables).
pg089_n0010: Like all the other special journals, posting entries from the sales journal is done in two stages as follows:
pg089_n0011: Stage one: Posting to a subsidiary ledger
pg089_n0013: Posting to a subsidiary ledger involves posting the entries to the individual accounts of each customer who appears in the journal.
pg089_n0014: The entries are recorded on the debit side of the respective accounts (personal accounts of each customer).
pg089_n0015: This is because the transactions involved are the increases in assets (receivables from each respective customer).
pg089_n0016: Stage two: Posting to the general ledger
pg089_n0018: The general ledger posting involves the periodic (weekly or monthly) record of the total from the journal.
pg089_n0019: These are posted to the sales account and the trade receivables account as they represent increases in revenues (sales) and trade receivables, respectively.
pg089_n0020: Therefore, the trade receivables accounts will be debited, while the sales accounts will be credited.
pg089_n0025: Posting from the sales returns journal
pg089_n0027: The sales returns journal records returns of goods from credit customers.
pg089_n0028: These transactions lead to a decrease in revenue (sales are decreased by sales returns) and a decrease in assets (trade receivables).
pg089_n0029: Like all the other special journals, posting entries from the sales returns journal is done in two stages as follows:
pg089_n0030: Stage one: Posting to a subsidiary ledger
pg089_n0032: Posting to a subsidiary ledger involves posting the entries to the individual accounts of each customer in the journal.
pg089_n0033: The entries are made on the credit side of the respective accounts (personal accounts of each customer).
pg089_n0034: This is because the transactions involved decreases the assets (receivables from each customer).
pg090_n0003: Stage two: Posting to the general ledger
pg090_n0005: The general ledger posting involves the periodic (weekly or monthly) totals of the journal.
pg090_n0006: These are posted to the sales returns account and the trade receivables account as they represent decreases in revenues (sales, through returns) and assets, respectively.
